title: git & GitHub
text:
What is git? 🔧
git is a distributed version control system created by Linus Torvalds (the Linux creator) in 2005
Key concepts:

Repository (repo): A project folder tracked by git
Commit: A snapshot of your project at a point in time
Branch: An independent line of development
Remote: A version of your repository hosted elsewhere (e.g., GitHub)







git vs GitHub


git = The version control software (runs on your computer) – you must install
GitHub = A website/service for hosting git repositories (plus collaboration tools) – you must make an account

title: git & GitHub
text:
git’s Philosophy 🌳
Distributed version control means:

Everyone has a complete copy of the project history
Work offline - you don’t need constant internet connection
Fast operations - most things happen locally
Backup by design - multiple complete copies exist

The git workflow:
Working Directory → Staging Area → Local Repository → Remote Repository
Key advantage: You can experiment locally without affecting others until you’re ready to share!

title: git & GitHub
text:
* Understanding merge 🔗
Merging combines changes from different branches
# Switch to main branch
git checkout main

# Merge feature branch
git merge new-feature
What happens:

git combines the changes
Creates a merge commit (usually)
Both histories are preserved

Possible outcomes:

Fast-forward: Clean merge, just moves pointer
Merge commit: Creates new commit combining both branches
Conflict: Manual intervention needed (we’ll discuss next)

title: git & GitHub
text:
Dealing with Conflicts ⚠️
Conflicts occur when same lines are edited differently
When you see a conflict:
git merge new-feature
# Auto-merging file.txt
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in file.txt
# Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
The file will look like:
<<<<<<< HEAD
Your version of the line
=======
Their version of the line
>>>>>>> new-feature
To resolve:

Open the file
Decide what to keep
Remove the conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>)
Stage and commit

git add file.txt
git commit -m "Resolve merge conflict"

title: Problem Set Solutions: Data Wrangling in Python
text:
Step 1: Download from FRED
Go to FRED and search for two series, e.g.:

UNRATE — US Unemployment Rate (monthly)
CPIAUCSL — US CPI (monthly, use pct_change(12) to get year-on-year inflation)

Download both as CSV files. Each will have two columns: DATE and a value column.

title: Problem Set Solutions: Data Wrangling in Python
section: Step 2: Load and standardise the date column
text:
Step 2: Load and standardise the date column
import pandas as pd

unemp = pd.read_csv("UNRATE.csv")
cpi   = pd.read_csv("CPIAUCSL.csv")

# Convert DATE to datetime — always do this explicitly
unemp["DATE"] = pd.to_datetime(unemp["DATE"])
cpi["DATE"]   = pd.to_datetime(cpi["DATE"])

title: Problem Set Solutions: Data Wrangling in Python
text:
Step 3: Merge on date
df = pd.merge(unemp, cpi, on="DATE", how="outer")
df = df.sort_values("DATE").reset_index(drop=True)

title: Problem Set Solutions: Data Wrangling in Python
text:
Step 4: Diagnose frequency mismatches
If one series is monthly and another is quarterly, you’ll see gaps after the merge. Check with:
print(df.isnull().sum())
print(df["DATE"].diff().value_counts())   # shows time gaps
To align frequencies, resample to quarterly:
df = df.set_index("DATE")
df_quarterly = df.resample("QS").mean()   # take mean within each quarter

title: Problem Set Solutions: Data Wrangling in Python
text:
Step 5: Dual-axis line plot
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))

# Left axis: unemployment
ax1.plot(df_quarterly.index, df_quarterly["UNRATE"], color="steelblue", label="Unemployment")
ax1.set_ylabel("Unemployment Rate (%)", color="steelblue")

# Right axis: inflation
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.plot(df_quarterly.index, df_quarterly["inflation"], color="firebrick", label="Inflation")
ax2.set_ylabel("Inflation (%)", color="firebrick")

ax1.set_title("US Unemployment and Inflation Over Time")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

A Stylised Economic Data Project
A typical economic data analysis project might consist of:

Version control: tracking all changes
Data collection: often scraping or API calls
Data cleaning: wrangling raw data into usable form
Analysis and generation of results: running models
Presentation: tables, figures, reports
Replication materials: packaging everything for others

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041

It is very unlikely that you would want to use a single tool for all steps. A realistic project might look like:



Step
Tool

git / GitHub

Presentation

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Why Automate the Full Pipeline?
Ideally we would like to:

Automate the process completely or as much as possible

What if next month you want to update the data at step 1?
What if a collaborator suggests a different cleaning step?

Remember what was done in previous versions to revert if needed







Note


The first is about designing an efficient replication process (e.g., a Makefile); the second is version control (git), which we have already covered.

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Workflow: make 🛠️
make is a Unix tool that specifies the full path a project follows: rather than running steps one by one, you run the Makefile with a single command

The key value-add: make only runs steps that are necessary
If nothing prior to step \(x\) has been altered, make detects this and only runs steps \(x, x+1, \ldots\)
A very complete discussion of Make with examples is provided by Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
Gentzkow & Shapiro also have a nice discussion of shell script alternatives (chapter 2 here)
Do not feel like you must do this (it is the advanced solution), but you need something to oversee the entire project

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
A Simple Makefile Example
# Makefile for a data analysis project

all: output/results.pdf

data/clean.csv: src/clean.py data/raw.csv
    python src/clean.py

output/results.csv: src/analysis.py data/clean.csv
    python src/analysis.py

output/results.pdf: report/paper.qmd output/results.csv
    quarto render report/paper.qmd
Running make from the project root re-runs only what has changed. This is the foundation of a reproducible pipeline.

text:
Modern Alternatives: Snakemake & DVC
make is powerful but dated. Modern alternatives exist:

Snakemake: Python-native workflow manager, popular in bioinformatics and increasingly in economics; handles parallelism cleanly
DVC (Data Version Control): extends git to handle large data files and ML pipelines; integrates with cloud storage
Prefect / Airflow: for production-grade orchestration

For many research projects, we may be happy with just some runner file like runAll.py, but we need something to automate “build”.

Documentation: Why It Matters






Tip


“You will probably spend more time reading code than writing code.” — Jesús Fernández-Villaverde



Research projects should be documented extensively:

Globally — using a README file at the project root
Locally — commenting within scripts

Both are important; neither alone is sufficient.

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Commenting in Scripts
All serious programming languages allow inline comments:

Comments are instructions for human readers – the machine ignores them (well, it used to…)
Should be used throughout wherever something is not immediately obvious
At minimum, section-level explanations should always be present
Comments should be maintained alongside code: stale comments are misleading
Err on the side of verbosity future you will thank present you!

# We merge the household survey (hhsurvey) with the administrative records (admin)
# using the household ID (hh_id). Some households appear only in one source;

README Files
A README file in the main directory gives global instructions for a project:

Explains procedures followed from start to finish
Lists external libraries/dependencies needed
Describes the directory structure
Provides contact details and citation information







Note


This should be the first thing you look for when you download someone else’s code. It may be called README, README.txt, README.md, …



A good short resource on README best practices is available here.

Consistency in structure matters as much as content. A typical economic project might look like:
project/
├── README.md
├── Makefile
├── data/
│   ├── raw/          ← never modified after collection
│   └── clean/        ← output of cleaning scripts
├── src/
│   ├── 01_clean.py
│   ├── 02_analysis.py

├── output/
│   ├── tables/
│   └── figures/

Consistent Style
There are many frequently used stylistic choices in programming – often not enforced by syntax but still very important:

People develop preferred directory structures for projects
Delimiter choices for data (commas, tabs, pipes)
Spacing in code is often user-specific (though some languages enforce rules)
Intelligent variable naming simplifies work considerably







Tip


Even if there are no rules, internal consistency is key: it enables re-use of standardised code and reduces cognitive load.

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Spacing and Line Length
In some languages, spacing is syntactically significant:

Python uses indentation to delimit loops and conditional blocks
Fortran reserves initial spaces for particular statements
The convention of not exceeding 80 characters per line is very common. We may ask: Why?



Institutions are ingrained and slow to change!

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Python Style: PEP 8 & Beyond
Python has an official style guide: PEP 8
Key recommendations: - 4 spaces for indentation (never tabs) - Maximum line length of 79 characters (PEP 8) or 88 (Black formatter) - Two blank lines between top-level functions/classes - One blank line between methods
Tooling that enforces this automatically:

black: opinionated auto-formatter (“the uncompromising code formatter”)
ruff: extremely fast linter + formatter-
flake8: linter (catches style and logic errors)

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Variable Naming
Variable naming is itself a form of documentation:

Good naming makes things dramatically easier; bad naming is a disaster
Consider a binary variable for sex at birth — potential names: {var1, gender, female}
Conventions: snake_case (Python standard) or camelCase (more common in JS/Java)
Consistency within a project is essential

text:
The Core Idea
Where possible, automation (avoiding human interaction) and abstraction (writing code flexible for many circumstances) should be embraced:

Consider calculating \(E(Y) = \sum_{x=x_{\min}}^{x_{\max}} E(Y|X=x) \cdot P(X=x)\)
One could tabulate \(X\) and compute expected values by hand
Better: iterate through all values of \(X\) automatically (AUTOMATION)
Best: write a function to do this for any two variables (ABSTRACTION)

def conditional_expectation(df, outcome, conditioning_var):
    """Compute E[outcome] via law of iterated expectations."""
    probs = df[conditioning_var].value_counts(normalize=True)
    cond_means = df.groupby(conditioning_var)[outcome].mean()
    return (cond_means * probs).sum()

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Why Functions?
Writing functions is central to both automation and abstraction:

Separates and re-uses key code blocks
Allows focus on perfecting code once, then reusing optimised versions
Everything in a research project should be replicable by machine







Warning


If you ever find yourself typing commands into a Python shell thinking “I’ll remember what I did”… you are in trouble. Write it down as a script!

LLMs and Workflow: Opportunities and Risks
AI coding assistants (GitHub Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT) have become a real part of modern workflows:
Opportunities:

Accelerate boilerplate code writing

Translate across languages (e.g., Stata → Python)

Risks:

Can obscure understanding if used as a crutch

Three Questions Every Programmer Faces
As soon as you have written some code:



Question
Term




My code runs, but does it do what it should?
Testing


My code does not run. Why?
Debugging


My code runs very slowly. Why?
Profiling



These are distinct activities requiring distinct approaches.

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Testing
Testing is a constant process requiring vigilance:

In empirical applications, test whether code returns correct values on simulated data where the answer is known
Test modularly: each script should be tested standalone
Similarly, each argument to a function should be tested
Consider proactively building in assertions:

def compute_unemployment_rate(n_unemployed, n_labour_force):
    rate = 100 * n_unemployed / n_labour_force
    assert 0 <= rate <= 100, f"Rate {rate:.1f}% is out of bounds — check inputs"
    return rate
Modern Python: use pytest for systematic test suites.

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Debugging
Debugging refers to finding errors that prevent a script from running:

Read error messages carefully: they usually tell you what went wrong and where
Consult the documentation as a first step
As a last resort, paste the exact error into a search engine (or ask an LLM)
Warnings: even when a script runs — should be investigated; they often signal inefficiencies or incorrect results







Tip


Do not think that just because a script runs, it is correct. Always return to testing.

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
An Application: Causal Forests
To see an example of a complete stylised project, let’s consider heterogeneity in some treatment effect:

This is more on the modelling side of data science
We will use a tool from causal machine learning known as causal forests (Athey, Tibshirani & Wager, 2019; Wager & Athey, 2018)
We will briefly discuss the econometrics at a high level
Note: this course is not about formal modelling – if you find this interesting, please consider taking further ML and causal econometrics courses (very happy to talk about this with you in office hours)!

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
section: The Starting Point: Average Treatment Effect (ATE) 📐
text:
The Starting Point: Average Treatment Effect (ATE) 📐
We are often interested in pinning down an average treatment effect (ATE):

Provides the impact of some treatment on outcomes in a population
Formally defined as: \(\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]\)
If treatment is assigned exogenously (e.g., randomly): \(\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}[Y_i|T_i=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i|T_i=0]\)
i.e., the treatment effect is simply the difference in mean outcomes between those treated and not
This is often already a challenging parameter to nail down!

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) 🎯
But, we also care about heterogeneity: who gains and who loses from an intervention?
\[\text{CATE}(X) = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X]\]

Measures the average treatment effect conditioned on covariates \(X\)
Provides insight into how treatment effects vary across subgroups
Policy relevance: targeting interventions to those who benefit most







Note


This is a significantly harder parameter to estimate than the ATE: standard regression struggles because of overfitting and the “curse of dimensionality”.

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
section: Why Can’t We Just Use OLS?
text:
Why Can’t We Just Use OLS?
Consider estimating \(\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]\) by running separate regressions within subgroups:

With many covariates, cells become very thin
Partitioning is arbitrary (which variables? how many bins?)
OLS with interactions: degrees of freedom collapse rapidly

Machine learning offers tools to learn heterogeneous effects from data in a disciplined way — this is where causal forests come in.

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Causal Forests: A Rough Overview 🌳
A random forest learns heterogeneity via recursive partitioning of the data:

Causal forests extend random forests for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects (Wager & Athey, 2018; Athey, Tibshirani & Wager, 2019)
We ask the data: which units are most similar in terms of their treatment effects?
Effectively: split data to find units with the most similar effects, building up a “tree”
Each decision tree is trained to partition data based on covariates and treatment assignments
Each tree “learns” the relationship between features, treatment, and outcome

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
The Honest Tree
A key insight in causal forests: honesty

Standard trees are “greedy”: they can overfit to the training data
Causal forests use sample splitting: one half finds the best partition (tree structure), the other half estimates treatment effects within leaves
This avoids in-sample bias and yields valid confidence intervals
The forest then aggregates many such honest trees to reduce variance







Tip


This is what separates causal machine learning from predictive ML: we want valid inference, not just low prediction error.

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
What is Webscraping?
Essentially: harvesting data stored on the web in irregular or highly dispersed format

When undertaking economic/data science analysis, we want regular data in rows and columns
The web contains vast amounts of data that has never been packaged as a clean CSV
Webscraping is the process of collecting and structuring it







Note


Two general steps: 1. Loop through nested URLs to reach many source HTML pages 2. Parse HTML (or JSON, XML) and format into a usable structure

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
section: Why is This Useful for Economists?
text:
Why is This Useful for Economists?
Often data is not stored as a CSV or standardised format:

In some cases, data does not exist in any centralised form
This opens up entirely new types of data we might not have considered
The majority of economics papers now use “novel” data (i.e., not purely survey-based)

Real examples from my own work (simple real-use cases):

Downloading, unzipping and merging 1,000+ DHS surveys, up-to-date at the moment of scraping
Downloading all 30,000+ NBER working papers for text analysis
Downloading election results: India, Philippines
Collecting standardised statistics across many geographies and time periods

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Economics Papers Using Scraped Data
Notable examples in the literature:

“The Billion Prices Project” — Cavallo & Rigobon (2016): online prices scraped from hundreds of retailers to measure inflation in real time
“Nowcasting the Local Economy” — Glaeser et al. (2017): Yelp data scraped to measure local economic activity
“Measuring Economic Policy Uncertainty” — Baker, Bloom & Davis (2016): automated text analysis of newspaper archives
“Do Expiring Budgets Lead to Wasteful Spending?” — Liebman & Mahoney (2017): federal contracting data scraped from USASpending.gov
Many others: see Table 1 of Edelman (JEP, 2012)

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
Three Considerations Before You Scrape
Before starting any webscraping project, ask:

Is the target standardised enough?
Are there legal limits?
Are there technical limits?

Also: do you even need to scrape?

Some websites provide data in a central download option already
Many sites have APIs (sometimes free, sometimes paid) that make the task much easier
The site IDEAS/RePEc is a great example of this
Owners of sites are sometimes happy to provide data upon request

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
1. Is the Target Standardised Enough?
Webscraping requires interacting with source code (HTML or XML) of websites:

Much harder if you are scraping many disparate websites rather than many pages within a single site
More challenging if the source format changes over time (e.g., PDFs in early years, machine-readable in later years)
Some websites are stored on unstable servers — plan for failures







Tip


A good webscraping script handles errors gracefully — use try/except blocks and build in retry logic. Never assume a request will succeed.

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
2. Are There Legal Limits?
Some websites do not allow webscraping — either because they consider information proprietary, or to prevent robot traffic from overloading their servers:

The law is complex and jurisdiction-dependent
There are legal precedents — e.g., hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn (US Ninth Circuit, 2022) found scraping publicly accessible data to be lawful, but this varies by context
Where possible: seek permission, read Terms of Service
Always check the robots.txt file (e.g., https://example.com/robots.txt)

# robots.txt example
User-agent: *
Disallow: /private/
Crawl-delay: 10

title: Workflow, Modelling & Webscraping: BEE2041
text:
3. Are There Technical Limits?
Many websites have safeguards against excessive crawling (CAPTCHAs, rate limiting, IP blocking):

Simple limit: rate limiting – slow down your requests
IP blocking: more serious; could use proxies, but this is technically non-trivial
CAPTCHAs_ “Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart” – designed specifically to block automated access







Important


Be a polite scraper: add delays between requests (time.sleep()), identify your bot in headers, and never hammer a server.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
The Problem with Files


Suppose you are managing data for a university. You might have:

A spreadsheet of students and their grades
A spreadsheet of courses and lecturers
A spreadsheet of student enrolments

This is a file processing system — and it starts to break down fast.
Think about:

A library managing millions of books and members
A company tracking employees, sales, inventory
A university managing students, modules, grades, staff

What could go wrong?


Source: xkcd.com/2116

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
File Processing Systems: The Problems
A file processing system stores data categorically with all required data for particular uses in individual files.
It has some advantages: it is cheap and easy to use. But it has serious disadvantages:

Data redundancy — the same data stored in multiple places
Data inconsistency — copies get out of sync
Data isolation — data in separate files hard to combine
Program dependence — data format tied to specific programs
Atomicity issues — partial updates leave data corrupted
Data security — hard to control who sees what

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Database Management Systems: The Solution
A DBMS = Database + Management System

Database: a structured, organised collection of related data
Management System: the software that stores, retrieves, updates, and secures that data

Advantages over flat files:

No redundant data — a fact is stored once, in one place
Data consistency and integrity — rules are enforced automatically
Data security and privacy — fine-grained access control
Easy, fast access — the DBMS does the heavy lifting
Easy recovery from failures
Flexible and scalable — add tables, users, and data without restructuring

title: Relational Database Management Systems
section: What Exactly is a Relational Database?
text:
What Exactly is a Relational Database?


A relational database organises data into tables (also called relations).
Each table has:

Columns (attributes): the fields, e.g. Lec_name, Lec_dept
Rows (tuples): the individual records, e.g. one lecturer

Tables are linked to each other through keys: shared columns that create explicit relationships.
This is the “relational” in relational database: the data model is built on the mathematical concept of a relation (from set theory).
RDBMS = Relational Database Management System: the software that implements this model.

Example: two related tables

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
What is SQL?
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language we use to talk to a relational database.
It was originally called Structured English Query Language (SEQUEL), and the name reflects its design: SQL reads like natural English.
SELECT Lec_name, Lec_dept
FROM   Lecturer
WHERE  Lec_dept = 'Economics';
Read it out loud: “Select the name and department from the Lecturer table where the department is Economics.”
SQL is:

Declarative: you say what you want, not how to get it
Standardised_ the core language works across PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and more
Universal: more or less every data scientist, analyst, and data engineer uses it

title: Relational Database Management Systems
section: SQL and RDBMS: How They Fit Together
text:
SQL and RDBMS: How They Fit Together


Think of the RDBMS as the system, and SQL as the way you access the system.

The RDBMS stores and manages data (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL…)
SQL is the language you use to drive it
You type SQL; the RDBMS figures out how to execute it efficiently

SQL covers four main areas:



Area
Abbreviation

Define structure

CREATE TABLE, DROP


Query data

Modify data

DML: modifying data

Bringing it into Python

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
The Math Behind It All


There is substantial theory behind DBMS… more than you might expect.
This is captured in Data Models, which formalise what data are and how they relate to each other.
At a conceptual level, we describe data using an Entity-Relationship (E-R) Diagram.
At a practical level, this leads to the RDBMS model we use today, first described formally by E. F. Codd in a landmark 1970 IBM paper.
We will encounter a piece of this mathematics: relational algebra, when we discuss JOINs.
If you want to explore E-R diagrams further, see: geeksforgeeks.org/introduction-of-er-model/

Edgar F. Codd (1923-2003)

Born in Portland, Dorset, UK
Worked at IBM’s San Jose Research Lab
1970 paper: “A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks”
Won the Turing Award in 1981

Everything we do with SQL ultimately traces back to his work.
Wikipedia: Edgar F. Codd

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
RDBMS: The Building Blocks
A Relational Database Management System consists of:



Concept
What it means




Table (relation)
A 2D structure of rows and columns


Record (tuple)
One row in a table


Field (attribute)
One column: a named data item


Domain
The set of allowed values for a field


Schema
The structure/blueprint of the database


Instance
The actual data in the database at a point in time


Keys
Special fields used to identify and link records

title: Relational Database Management Systems
section: Keys: The Glue of Relational Databases
text:
Keys: The Glue of Relational Databases
Keys are fundamental to how tables relate to each other:

Super key: any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row
Candidate key: a minimal super key (no redundant attributes)
Primary key: the chosen candidate key for a table – must be unique and NOT NULL
Foreign key: a field in one table that references the primary key of another

CREATE TABLE Lecturer (
  Lec_ID   TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  Lec_name TEXT,
  Lec_dept TEXT
);
CREATE TABLE Module (
  Mod_code TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  Mod_name TEXT,
  Lec_ID   TEXT,
  FOREIGN KEY (Lec_ID) REFERENCES Lecturer(Lec_ID)
);

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Constraints
Constraints enforce the rules of your data:



Constraint
Meaning




NOT NULL
Field cannot be empty


UNIQUE
No two rows can have the same value


PRIMARY KEY
Unique + Not null: identifies each row


FOREIGN KEY
Must match a value in another table (or be NULL)


CHECK
Value must satisfy a condition


DEFAULT
Provides a default value when none is given



These make your database self-enforcing. Bad data cannot be inserted.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Cardinality: How Tables Relate
Cardinality describes the numerical relationship between records in two tables:

One-to-one: One lecturer has one office; one office has one lecturer
One-to-many: One lecturer teaches many modules; each module has one lecturer
Many-to-many: Students enrol in many modules; modules have many students

In our teaching database:

Lecturer → Module is one-to-many (one lecturer, many modules)
A student-module enrolment would be many-to-many

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
A Note on Normalisation
Why do we have multiple tables instead of one big table?
This is the idea behind normalisation: organising data to reduce redundancy and improve integrity.
Informally:

Don’t store the same fact in more than one place
Each table should describe one thing
Dependencies should be explicit via keys

For example: if Abdul’s department changes, we update it in one row of Lecturer, not in every row of Module.
See https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dbms/introduction-of-database-normalization/ for further information.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
What is SQLite3?
SQLite is a lightweight, serverless relational database engine.

No separate database server to install or run
The entire database lives in a single file on disk
Built into Python: no extra install needed
Powers many common applications: Firefox, Android, iOS, WhatsApp, and more

For learning SQL and for many real data science tasks, SQLite3 is perfect:
"SQLite is the most widely deployed database engine in the world"
-- SQLite documentation
We will start by working directly from the command line – the same way this is often done in practice.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
The SQLite3 Shell: Getting In
Open a terminal and launch SQLite3 with a database filename:
# Creates teaching.db if it doesn't exist, opens it if it does
sqlite3 teaching.db
You are now inside the interactive shell. The prompt changes to:
SQLite version 3.x.x
Enter ".help" for usage hints.
sqlite>
To exit at any time:
sqlite> .quit
Note: SQLite3 only creates the .db file once data is written to it. Simply opening is not enough.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Essential Dot Commands
The SQLite3 shell has special “dot commands” that control the session – not SQL, but very useful for us:
.help              -- list all dot commands
.tables            -- list all tables in the database
.schema            -- show CREATE statements for all tables
.schema Lecturer   -- show CREATE for one specific table
.headers on        -- show column names in query output
.mode column       -- align output in neat columns
.mode table        -- pretty-print with box borders
.width 20 20 15    -- set column widths manually
.read script.sql   -- run a SQL script file
.output file.txt   -- redirect query output to a file
.quit              -- exit the shell
Worth running .headers on and .mode column at the start of a session – the raw pipe-separated output can be hard to read.

sqlite3 teaching.db

------  --------  ----------------
L211    Abdul     Computer Science
L555    Sarah     Economics
L179    Amy       Physics
L234    Lou       Psychology
R101    Marco     Social Science

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
SQL: Structured Query Language
SQL (pronounced “S-Q-L” or “sequel”) was originally Structured English Query Language.
The name emphasises the natural, English-like syntax: reading a SQL query should feel like reading a sentence.
SQL includes four main sub-languages:



Sub-language
Abbreviation
What it does




Data Definition Language
DDL
CREATE, DROP, ALTER tables


Data Query Language
DQL
SELECT data


Data Manipulation Language
DML
INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE rows


Data Control Language
DCL
GRANT, REVOKE permissions



Today we focus on DDL, DQL, and DML.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
section: SQL Syntax: The Anatomy of a Query
text:
SQL Syntax: The Anatomy of a Query
A SQL query has a predictable structure:
SELECT   column1, column2, ...       -- what to retrieve
FROM     table_name                  -- where to look
WHERE    condition                   -- filter rows
GROUP BY column                      -- aggregate groups
HAVING   condition                   -- filter groups
ORDER BY column ASC|DESC             -- sort results
LIMIT    n;                          -- restrict number of rows
Not all clauses are required — SELECT ... FROM ... is the minimum.
The best way to understand SQL is to use it!

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Basic SELECT
-- All columns from Lecturer
SELECT * FROM Lecturer;

Lec_ID  Lec_name  Lec_dept
------  --------  ----------------
L211    Abdul     Computer Science
L555    Sarah     Economics
L179    Amy       Physics
L234    Lou       Psychology
R101    Marco     Social Science
-- Specific columns only
SELECT Lec_name, Lec_dept FROM Lecturer;

Lec_name  Lec_dept
--------  ----------------
Abdul     Computer Science
Sarah     Economics
...

text:
Aliases and Calculated Fields
-- Rename columns in output with AS
SELECT Lec_name AS Name,
       Lec_dept AS Department
FROM   Lecturer;

Name   Department
-----  ----------------
Abdul  Computer Science
Sarah  Economics
Amy    Physics
Lou    Psychology
Marco  Social Science
Aliases make output cleaner and are essential in JOINs where column names from different tables can clash.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
WHERE: Filtering Rows
-- Lecturers in Computer Science
SELECT *
FROM   Lecturer
WHERE  Lec_dept = 'Computer Science';

Lec_ID  Lec_name  Lec_dept
------  --------  ----------------
L211    Abdul     Computer Science
-- Modules taught by L211
SELECT *
FROM   Module
WHERE  Lec_ID = 'L211';

Mod_code  Mod_name     Lec_ID
--------  -----------  ------
C01       Intro to CS  L211
C02       DBMS         L211

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
WHERE with Multiple Conditions
-- AND: both conditions must be true
SELECT *
FROM   Lecturer
WHERE  Lec_dept != 'Physics'
AND    Lec_ID   != 'R101';
-- OR: either condition true
SELECT *
FROM   Module
WHERE  Lec_ID = 'L211' OR Lec_ID = 'L179';
-- IS NULL: find unassigned modules
SELECT *
FROM   Module
WHERE  Lec_ID IS NULL;

Mod_code  Mod_name      Lec_ID
--------  ------------  ------
U01       Dissertation
WHERE Lec_ID = NULL does not work. Always use IS NULL.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
ORDER BY, LIMIT, and LIKE
-- Sort alphabetically by name
SELECT   Lec_name, Lec_dept
FROM     Lecturer
ORDER BY Lec_name ASC;
-- First 3 modules by code
SELECT   *
FROM     Module
ORDER BY Mod_code
LIMIT    3;
-- % is a wildcard meaning "any characters"
SELECT * FROM Module
WHERE  Mod_name LIKE '%Data%';

Mod_code  Mod_name      Lec_ID
--------  ------------  ------
C22       Data Science  L179

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Aggregate Functions
SQL provides built-in functions that summarise data:



Function
What it does




COUNT(*)
Count all rows


COUNT(col)
Count non-NULL values in a column


SUM(col)
Sum values


AVG(col)
Average


MIN(col)
Minimum value


MAX(col)
Maximum value



SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_lecturers FROM Lecturer;

total_lecturers
---------------
5

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
GROUP BY: Aggregating by Category
-- How many modules does each lecturer teach?
SELECT   Lec_ID,
         COUNT(*) AS num_modules
FROM     Module
WHERE    Lec_ID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Lec_ID
ORDER BY num_modules DESC;

Lec_ID  num_modules
------  -----------
L211    2
L179    2
L555    1

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
HAVING: Filtering Groups
HAVING is like WHERE but applied after aggregation:
-- Only lecturers teaching more than 1 module
SELECT   Lec_ID,
         COUNT(*) AS num_modules
FROM     Module
WHERE    Lec_ID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Lec_ID
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 1;

Lec_ID  num_modules
------  -----------
L211    2
L179    2
A common confusion: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Why JOIN?
Our data is spread across two tables. To answer most interesting questions we need to combine them. This is what JOINs do (we have of course seen this before…).







SQL JOIN
What it keeps




INNER JOIN
Only rows with a match in both tables


LEFT JOIN
All rows from the left table; NULLs for non-matches on the right


RIGHT JOIN
All rows from the right table (SQLite: use reversed LEFT JOIN)


FULL OUTER JOIN
All rows from both tables (not in SQLite, but can be achieved)



The SQL JOIN corresponds directly to the relational algebra bowtie operator ⋈.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
A Mental Model for JOINs
Before writing any JOIN, ask two questions:

Which table am I primarily interested in? → That table goes on the LEFT (or is the “base”)
What should happen to rows with no match? → If you want them kept (with NULLs), use LEFT JOIN; if you want them dropped, use INNER JOIN



“Give me all modules, and attach lecturer info where available”
→ Module LEFT JOIN Lecturer (keeps Dissertation with NULL lecturer)

“Give me only modules that have a lecturer”
→ Module INNER JOIN Lecturer (drops Dissertation)

Getting the JOIN type wrong is one of the most common sources of silently wrong results in data work. Always check row counts!

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
INNER JOIN: Only Matching Rows
SELECT   m.Mod_code,
         m.Mod_name,
         l.Lec_name,
         l.Lec_dept
FROM     Module    AS m
INNER JOIN Lecturer AS l
  ON m.Lec_ID = l.Lec_ID
ORDER BY l.Lec_name;

Mod_code  Mod_name          Lec_name  Lec_dept
--------  ----------------  --------  ----------------
C22       Data Science      Amy       Physics
C39       Computer Networks Amy       Physics
C01       Intro to CS       Abdul     Computer Science
C02       DBMS              Abdul     Computer Science
E15       Econometrics      Sarah     Economics
U01 (NULL Lec_ID) and Marco (no modules) are both excluded.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
LEFT JOIN: Keep All Modules
SELECT   m.Mod_code,
         m.Mod_name,
         l.Lec_name,
         l.Lec_dept
FROM     Module    AS m
LEFT JOIN Lecturer AS l
  ON m.Lec_ID = l.Lec_ID
ORDER BY m.Mod_code;

Mod_code  Mod_name          Lec_name  Lec_dept
--------  ----------------  --------  ----------------
C01       Intro to CS       Abdul     Computer Science
C02       DBMS              Abdul     Computer Science
C22       Data Science      Amy       Physics
C39       Computer Networks Amy       Physics
E15       Econometrics      Sarah     Economics
U01       Dissertation
U01 now appears with NULLs for lecturer columns. All modules are retained.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
section: Simulating a RIGHT JOIN in SQLite
text:
Simulating a RIGHT JOIN in SQLite
SQLite does not support RIGHT JOIN – swap the tables in a LEFT JOIN:
-- All lecturers, including those with no modules
SELECT   l.Lec_name,
         l.Lec_dept,
         m.Mod_code,
         m.Mod_name
FROM     Lecturer AS l
LEFT JOIN Module  AS m
  ON l.Lec_ID = m.Lec_ID
ORDER BY l.Lec_name;

Lec_name  Lec_dept          Mod_code  Mod_name
--------  ----------------  --------  ----------------
Abdul     Computer Science  C01       Intro to CS
Abdul     Computer Science  C02       DBMS
Amy       Physics           C22       Data Science
Amy       Physics           C39       Computer Networks
Lou       Psychology
Marco     Social Science
Sarah     Economics         E15       Econometrics
Lou and Marco now appear with NULLs for module fields.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Understanding JOINs Visually


INNER JOIN — only matched rows
Lecturer   Module
  L211  ←→  C01
  L211  ←→  C02
  L179  ←→  C22
  L179  ←→  C39
  L555  ←→  E15
  L234  (no match) ✗
  R101  (no match) ✗
         U01 (NULL) ✗
Returns 5 rows.

LEFT JOIN — all from the left table
Module LEFT JOIN Lecturer: all 6 modules, U01 gets NULLs → 6 rows
Lecturer LEFT JOIN Module: all 6 lecturers, Lou and Marco get NULLs → 7 rows (Abdul and Amy appear twice)
Key insight: The table you want all rows from goes on the LEFT.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
JOIN with Aggregation
-- Modules taught per department (including zero counts)
SELECT   l.Lec_dept        AS Department,
         COUNT(m.Mod_code) AS Modules_Taught
FROM     Lecturer AS l
LEFT JOIN Module  AS m
  ON l.Lec_ID = m.Lec_ID
GROUP BY l.Lec_dept
ORDER BY Modules_Taught DESC;

Department        Modules_Taught
----------------  --------------
Computer Science  2
Physics           2
Economics         1
Psychology        0
Social Science    0
Using LEFT JOIN means departments with no modules still appear with a count of 0.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Subqueries
A subquery is a SELECT nested inside another statement:
-- Lecturers who teach at least one module
SELECT * FROM Lecturer
WHERE Lec_ID IN (
  SELECT DISTINCT Lec_ID FROM Module
  WHERE  Lec_ID IS NOT NULL
);
-- Lecturers with NO modules
SELECT * FROM Lecturer
WHERE Lec_ID NOT IN (
  SELECT DISTINCT Lec_ID FROM Module
  WHERE  Lec_ID IS NOT NULL
);

Lec_ID  Lec_name  Lec_dept
------  --------  --------------
L234    Lou       Psychology
R101    Marco     Social Science

The Math Behind SQL
Every SQL query corresponds to an operation in relational algebra — the formal mathematical foundation of SQL.



Operation

σ

You do not need to write relational algebra — but understanding it helps you reason about what SQL is doing.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
UNION: Combining Query Results
UNION stacks the results of two queries, removing duplicates. UNION ALL keeps them.
SELECT Lec_dept FROM Lecturer WHERE Lec_dept LIKE 'E%'
UNION
SELECT Lec_dept FROM Lecturer WHERE Lec_dept LIKE 'P%'
ORDER BY Lec_dept;

Lec_dept
--------
Economics
Physics
Psychology
Both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
Relational Database Management Systems
text:
UPDATE: Modifying Rows
-- Assign the Dissertation to Elena
UPDATE Module
SET    Lec_ID = 'L999'
WHERE  Mod_code = 'U01';

SELECT * FROM Module WHERE Mod_code = 'U01';
Mod_code  Mod_name      Lec_ID
--------  ------------  ------
U01       Dissertation  L999
⚠️ Always include a WHERE clause with UPDATE. Without it, every row in the table is modified, and there is no undo.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Foreign Key Constraints in Action
What happens if we try to delete Abdul, who has modules pointing at him?
By default, SQLite does not enforce foreign keys. You must turn it on:
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

DELETE FROM Lecturer WHERE Lec_ID = 'L211';
-- Error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed
Without the PRAGMA, the deletion silently succeeds. This leaves C01 and C02 pointing to a lecturer that no longer exists. These are called orphaned records and are a serious data integrity problem.
Always enable foreign key enforcement when your schema uses them.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Beyond SQLite: Databases on Servers
SQLite is a file-based database — the whole thing lives in one file on your local disk. This is great for learning and for many data science tasks.
But in the real world, you will often connect to a database running on a remote server:

A university or company database server
A cloud-hosted database (AWS RDS, Google Cloud SQL, Azure Database)
A shared research database you access over a network

The SQL you write is completely identical. Only the connection method changes.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
The Client-Server Model
Your laptop                    Database Server
  ┌────────────┐    network    ┌─────────────────┐
  │  SQL client│ ────────────► │  DB process     │
  │  (you!)    │ ◄──────────── │  (PostgreSQL,   │
  └────────────┘    results    │   MySQL, etc.)  │
                               └─────────────────┘

The server runs the database engine and holds all the data
The client (you) sends SQL queries and receives results
Communication happens over TCP/IP on a standard port
You authenticate with a username and password

Your client can be a command-line tool, a GUI app, or Python code – the server does not care which.

Connecting with psql and SSH
This is all quite advanced, but worth know it exists in case you come across this. View it as a “set-up cost”
psql is PostgreSQL’s command-line client – the direct equivalent of sqlite3:
# Connect to a remote server
psql -h db.university.ac.uk -p 5432 -U yourname -d researchdb
# You are prompted for a password; prompt becomes: researchdb=>
If the database is behind a firewall, tunnel through an SSH gateway:
# Step 1: forward the remote DB port to your local machine
ssh -L 5433:db.internal.university.ac.uk:5432 \
    yourname@ssh.university.ac.uk -N

# Step 2: in a new terminal, connect via the tunnel
psql -h localhost -p 5433 -U yourname -d researchdb
Once connected, the SQL you type is identical to what you have been writing today. The psql meta-commands differ slightly (.tables becomes \dt, .schema becomes \d tablename, .quit becomes \q) but everything else is the same.

import requests, pandas as pd, sqlite3
from functools import reduce

# The World Bank REST API: no library needed, just requests.
# Endpoint: /v2/country/all/indicator/{code}?format=json&per_page=20000&date=2010:2022
WB = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator"

indicators = {
    "NY.GDP.MKTP.CD": "gdp_usd",
    "NY.GDP.PCAP.CD": "gdp_pc_usd",
    "SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS": "unemp_pct",
    "SP.POP.TOTL":    "pop",
}

frames = []
for code, colname in indicators.items():
    r = requests.get(f"{WB}/{code}",
                     params={"format":"json","per_page":20000,"date":"2010:2022"})
    data = r.json()[1]          # [0] is pagination metadata, [1] is the data
    rows = [{"iso3":  d["countryiso3code"],
             "year":  int(d["date"]),
             colname: d["value"]}
            for d in data if d["countryiso3code"]]   # drop blanks
    frames.append(pd.DataFrame(rows))
    print(f"  {colname}: {len(frames[-1]):,} rows")

raw = reduce(lambda a, b: pd.merge(a, b, on=["iso3","year"], how="outer"), frames)
# Drop World Bank aggregate rows (iso3 codes that are not real countries)
raw = raw[raw["iso3"].str.len() == 3].copy()
print(f"\nMerged: {len(raw):,} country-year rows, {raw['iso3'].nunique()} countries")

Views: Saved Queries
A view is a named query stored in the database – it behaves like a table but recomputes its result each time it is queried:
CREATE VIEW vw_module_lecturer AS
SELECT m.Mod_code, m.Mod_name,
       l.Lec_name, l.Lec_dept
FROM   Module   AS m
JOIN   Lecturer AS l ON m.Lec_ID = l.Lec_ID;

-- Query it like a table
SELECT * FROM vw_module_lecturer WHERE Lec_dept = 'Physics';

Mod_code  Mod_name          Lec_name  Lec_dept

C22       Data Science      Amy       Physics
C39       Computer Networks Amy       Physics
Views are useful for: sharing consistent query logic, hiding complexity, and security (expose the view but not the underlying tables).

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Indexes: Making Queries Fast
For large databases, queries on unindexed columns require a full table scan: every row is checked.
-- On a 10-million-row table, this is slow without an index
SELECT * FROM GDP WHERE iso3 = 'GBR';

-- Create an index
CREATE INDEX idx_gdp_iso3 ON GDP(iso3);

-- Now the same query jumps straight to the right rows
SELECT * FROM GDP WHERE iso3 = 'GBR';
Rules of thumb:

Primary keys are indexed automatically
Index columns you filter on frequently (WHERE, JOIN ON)
Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes (the index must be maintained)
Do not over-index: each index costs storage and has performance implications

RDBMS require a pre-defined schema and structured data
What if data is semi-structured or schema-free? (JSON, logs, tweets, etc.)
What if you need to scale across hundreds of machines?

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
When to Use What?


Use SQL/RDBMS when:

Data is structured and relational
Data integrity is critical
You need complex queries and joins
Team knows SQL (everyone does!)
Examples: financial data, survey data, administrative records


Consider NoSQL when:

Data is unstructured or highly variable (web scraping, social media)
You need massive horizontal scalability
Write performance is critical at huge scale
Schema changes frequently

For most economics data science work: SQL is the right choice.

If you want to explore NoSQL: look up MongoDB – it stores data as JSON documents and is widely used.

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
A SQL Query Checklist
Before writing a complex query, ask yourself:

Which tables do I need? → FROM and JOIN
Which rows do I want? → WHERE
Which columns do I need? → SELECT
Do I need aggregation? → GROUP BY and HAVING
How should results be ordered? → ORDER BY
Are there NULL values I need to handle? → IS NULL, COALESCE

title: Relational Database Management Systems
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid
❌ UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause - affects every row, permanently
❌ WHERE col = NULL - always use IS NULL
❌ Confusing WHERE (before aggregation) and HAVING (after aggregation)
❌ Not enabling PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON in SQLite when your schema uses them
❌ Running large unfiltered queries on shared servers - use LIMIT to explore first
❌ Hardcoding passwords in scripts - use environment variables or .pgpass
❌ Forgetting that sqlite3 (the CLI tool) and SQLite3 (Python module) need their connections managed separately

text:
The Command Line 💻
The Command Line is also an interface (“CLI”), but provides a lower level way to interact with your OS

Trade-off between simplicity (GUIs) and flexibility (CLI)
Also you may hear these related concepts:

The Terminal: The text input and output environment
The Shell: The command line interpreter
BASH: The Linux and Mac default shell (Bourne Again SHell)
The Command Line: The physical line where commands are typed


Key point: The shell as we will think of it will refer to the BASH version
Windows note: Windows also has PowerShell, but BASH is the industry standard ✨

title: The Linux Command Line
section: Why Learn About the Command Line? 🎯
text:
Why Learn About the Command Line? 🎯
BASH in particular offers unique advantages:

Remarkable flexibility for OS-level operations

Often genuinely the fastest way to get tasks done
At times I access the command line from directly within other languages because it offers a faster way to do something

Helps you understand many other languages

Many command line style functions have been included in other higher-level languages
For example: ls, head, tail, pwd, cd, pipes (|), etc.

Some OS you will work with only have a command line interface
Most servers you work with will be running a version of BASH
Industry expectation: Data scientists are expected to be comfortable with command line 💼

title: The Linux Command Line
text:
The Unix Philosophy 🔧
The philosophy behind Linux/Unix, espoused by Thompson & Ritchie (early developers):

Write programs that do one thing and do it well

text:
Introduction to awk: Pattern Processing Language 🎓
What is awk?
awk is a complete programming language designed for text processing. It’s named after its creators: Aho, Weinberger, and Kernighan.
Why use awk? - Process structured data (columns/fields) - Perform calculations on data - Generate reports - Complex pattern matching and text transformation
Basic structure:
awk 'pattern { action }' file
Key concepts: - Automatically splits each line into fields (columns) - $1, $2, $3, … represent field 1, field 2, field 3, etc. - $0 represents the entire line - Default field separator is whitespace (spaces/tabs)

Changing field separator:
# Use semicolon as separator
awk -F ";" '{print $1}' data.csv

# Use comma (for CSV files)

# Multiple character separator
awk -F "::" '{print $2}' file.txt

# Print lines containing pattern

# Print specific column only for matching lines
awk '/2024/ {print $1, $5}' data.txt

# Print lines where column 3 > 100
awk '$3 > 100 {print}' data.txt

# Calculate sum of column 2
awk '{sum += $2} END {print sum}' numbers.txt

# Calculate average
awk '{sum += $2; count++} END {print sum/count}' numbers.txt

# Multiple conditions

title: SQL Teaching Exercises: Students, Modules & Lecturers
text:
3.1 Which students take which modules?
A three-way join across Enrolment, Student, and Module.
SELECT s.Stu_name,
       m.Mod_name
FROM   Enrolment e
JOIN   Student s ON e.Stu_ID   = s.Stu_ID
JOIN   Module  m ON e.Mod_code = m.Mod_code
ORDER BY s.Stu_name, m.Mod_name;
To also see the lecturer, extend the join. Frank is enrolled in U01 Dissertation which has Lec_ID = NULL – no lecturer is assigned. Depending on which join type you use, his Dissertation row is either dropped or kept:
-- INNER JOIN: Frank's Dissertation row is silently dropped
SELECT s.Stu_name, m.Mod_name, l.Lec_name
FROM   Enrolment e
JOIN   Student  s ON e.Stu_ID   = s.Stu_ID
JOIN   Module   m ON e.Mod_code = m.Mod_code
JOIN   Lecturer l ON m.Lec_ID   = l.Lec_ID
ORDER BY s.Stu_name;

-- LEFT JOIN: Frank's Dissertation row is kept, Lec_name shows NULL
SELECT s.Stu_name, m.Mod_name, l.Lec_name
FROM   Enrolment e
JOIN   Student    s ON e.Stu_ID   = s.Stu_ID
JOIN   Module     m ON e.Mod_code = m.Mod_code
LEFT JOIN Lecturer l ON m.Lec_ID  = l.Lec_ID
ORDER BY s.Stu_name;

Rule of thumb: use LEFT JOIN whenever the foreign key is optional, i.e. when NULL is a valid value in your schema.

title: SQL Teaching Exercises: Students, Modules & Lecturers
section: 3.2 How many modules does each student take?
text:
3.2 How many modules does each student take?
COUNT with GROUP BY: one row per student.
SELECT s.Stu_name,
       COUNT(e.Mod_code) AS modules_taken
FROM   Student s
LEFT JOIN Enrolment e ON s.Stu_ID = e.Stu_ID
GROUP BY s.Stu_ID, s.Stu_name
ORDER BY modules_taken DESC;

LEFT JOIN here means a student with no enrolments still appears with a count of 0 rather than being excluded entirely.

title: SQL Teaching Exercises: Students, Modules & Lecturers
section: 3.3 Which lecturers teach the most students?
text:
3.3 Which lecturers teach the most students?
We need COUNT(DISTINCT e.Stu_ID) rather than plain COUNT(*). Without DISTINCT, a student taking two of Abdul’s modules would be counted twice once per module. You may wish to run this counting totals including non-distinct matches to see differences.
SELECT l.Lec_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT e.Stu_ID) AS students_taught
FROM   Lecturer  l
JOIN   Module    m ON l.Lec_ID   = m.Lec_ID
JOIN   Enrolment e ON m.Mod_code = e.Mod_code
GROUP BY l.Lec_ID, l.Lec_name
ORDER BY students_taught DESC;

Marco (R101) does not appear — he has no modules, so the JOIN to Module produces no rows for him. Try changing the first JOIN to a LEFT JOIN to see what happens to his count.

title: SQL Teaching Exercises: Students, Modules & Lecturers
text:
3.4 Which lecturers have no students?
We can use a subquery for this… A subquery finds all lecturer IDs connected to at least one enrolment. NOT IN returns everyone outside that set.
SELECT Lec_name
FROM   Lecturer
WHERE  Lec_ID NOT IN (
    SELECT DISTINCT m.Lec_ID
    FROM   Module    m
    JOIN   Enrolment e ON m.Mod_code = e.Mod_code
    WHERE  m.Lec_ID IS NOT NULL
);

The WHERE m.Lec_ID IS NOT NULL guard is essential. If any Lec_ID in the subquery result is NULL, then NOT IN (..., NULL, ...) returns no rows at all: a common SQLite trap.

text:
4.1 SQLite foreign keys are OFF by default
Unlike most databases, SQLite does not enforce foreign key constraints unless you turn them on explicitly and the setting resets every time you open a new connection.
-- Check current state: 0 = off, 1 = on
PRAGMA foreign_keys;

title: SQL Teaching Exercises: Students, Modules & Lecturers
SQL Teaching Exercises: Students, Modules & Lecturers
text:
4.3 Deleting with enforcement enabled
-- Turn foreign key enforcement on for this session
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

-- The same delete is now blocked
DELETE FROM Lecturer WHERE Lec_ID = 'L211';
-- Error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON must be set every time you open SQLite. It does not persist between sessions.

text:
#STEP 1 - DATA LOADING & INSPECTION
# Step 1.a — Data Loading (Yahoo Finance)
# ----------------------------------------
# Goal: Pull raw daily market data for our variables:
# - BTC (crypto proxy)
# - NASDAQ (risk-on proxy)
# - DXY (USD strength proxy)
#
# Why we set START/END: reproducibility + consistent sample window

START = "2017-01-01"
END   = "2025-12-31"

# Yahoo ticker symbols (labels help readability later)
TICKERS = {
    "btc": "BTC-USD",     # Bitcoin price in USD
    "nasdaq": "^IXIC",    # NASDAQ Composite Index
    "dxy": "DX-Y.NYB"     # US Dollar Index (DXY)
}

import yfinance as yf
import pandas as pd

# Download daily OHLCV data:
# Open, High, Low, Close, Adj Close, Volume
# We keep raw output as *_raw so we don't overwrite cleaned data later
btc_raw = yf.download(TICKERS["btc"], start=START, end=END, auto_adjust=False, progress=False)
nasdaq_raw = yf.download(TICKERS["nasdaq"], start=START, end=END, auto_adjust=False, progress=False)
dxy_raw = yf.download(TICKERS["dxy"], start=START, end=END, auto_adjust=False, progress=False)

# Shape = (rows, columns)
# Rows = number of days available
# Columns ≈ 6 (OHLCV)
btc_raw.shape, nasdaq_raw.shape, dxy_raw.shape


# Step 1.b — Data Loading (FRED macro data)
# ----------------------------------------
# Fed Funds is a macroeconomic policy rate (monthly series in FRED).
# We use FRED because it is an official macro source and cleaner than Yahoo for rates.
# Later we will resample monthly → daily to align with BTC/NASDAQ/DXY.

from pandas_datareader import data as pdr

fed_raw = pdr.DataReader("FEDFUNDS", "fred", START, END)

# Shape here should be approx. (months, 1)
fed_raw.shape


# Step 1.c — Inspection & Wrangling Preparation
# ----------------------------------------
# Why reset_index():
# - yfinance returns Date as an index
# - we need Date as a column for merging (pd.merge requires a key column)
#
# Why flatten columns:
# - yfinance can return MultiIndex columns (e.g., ('Adj Close', 'BTC-USD'))
# - flattening ensures column names like "Adj Close" exist as plain text
# ----------------------------------------

def reset_and_flatten(df):
    df = df.reset_index()  # Date becomes a regular column
    if isinstance(df.columns, pd.MultiIndex):
        df.columns = df.columns.get_level_values(0)  # keep only first level (e.g., "Adj Close")
    return df

btc_raw = reset_and_flatten(btc_raw)
nasdaq_raw = reset_and_flatten(nasdaq_raw)
dxy_raw = reset_and_flatten(dxy_raw)

# Fed data already has simple columns, just reset index
fed_raw = fed_raw.reset_index()

# Quick inspection of column names (helps debugging and confirms structure)
btc_raw.columns, nasdaq_raw.columns, dxy_raw.columns, fed_raw.columns


# Step 1.d — Column Selection (Reduce dataset)
# ----------------------------------------
# We only need:
# - Date (merge key)
# - Adjusted Close (price level used for return calculations)
#
# Using Adj Close is standard because it accounts for corporate actions in equities.
# For Bitcoin, Close ≈ Adj Close, but we keep Adj Close for consistency.

btc = btc_raw[["Date", "Adj Close"]].rename(columns={"Adj Close": "btc_price"})
nasdaq = nasdaq_raw[["Date", "Adj Close"]].rename(columns={"Adj Close": "nasdaq_price"})
dxy = dxy_raw[["Date", "Adj Close"]].rename(columns={"Adj Close": "dxy_price"})

# Rename Fed columns for clarity
# FRED returns something like ["DATE", "FEDFUNDS"] after reset_index
fed_raw.columns = ["Date", "fed_rate"]
fed = fed_raw[["Date", "fed_rate"]]

# Quick preview (inspection step from lecture slides)
btc.head(), nasdaq.head(), dxy.head(), fed.head()


# Step 1.e — Data Type Cleaning (Datetime)
# ----------------------------------------
# Dates must match in type and format for:
# - merging
# - resampling
# - rolling window calculations

btc["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(btc["Date"])
nasdaq["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(nasdaq["Date"])
dxy["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(dxy["Date"])
fed["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(fed["Date"])


# Step 1.f — Data Quality Checks (Inspection)
# ----------------------------------------
# Before merging, we check:
# - missing values (NA)
# - duplicate dates (merge keys must be unique)
# These checks are important to avoid incorrect merges and biased results.

def quality_check(df, name):
    print(f"\n{name}")
    print("Missing values:\n", df.isna().sum())
    print("Duplicate dates:", df["Date"].duplicated().sum())
    print("Date range:", df["Date"].min(), "to", df["Date"].max())

quality_check(btc, "BTC")
quality_check(nasdaq, "NASDAQ")
quality_check(dxy, "DXY")
quality_check(fed, "FED FUNDS")


#STEP 2 — Data Cleaning & Alignment
# ----------------------------------------
# Step 2.a — Sort by Date + verify unique merge keys
# ----------------------------------------
# Why:
# - Sorting is good practice for time-series work (resample/rolling later)
# - Unique Date keys are required for a valid 1:1 merge

btc = btc.sort_values("Date").reset_index(drop=True)
nasdaq = nasdaq.sort_values("Date").reset_index(drop=True)
dxy = dxy.sort_values("Date").reset_index(drop=True)
fed = fed.sort_values("Date").reset_index(drop=True)

# Check duplicates (should be 0; if not, we must fix before merge)
btc["Date"].duplicated().sum(), nasdaq["Date"].duplicated().sum(), dxy["Date"].duplicated().sum(), fed["Date"].duplicated().sum()


# Step 2.b — Resample Fed Funds (monthly → daily)
# Why:
# - BTC/NASDAQ/DXY are daily series
# - FEDFUNDS is monthly
# - Resampling to daily + forward-fill means:
#   each day uses the most recently available policy rate until the next update

fed_daily = (
    fed.set_index("Date")
       .resample("D")      # create daily date index
       .ffill()            # forward-fill monthly values across days
       .reset_index()
)
fed_daily.head(), fed_daily.tail()


# Step 2.c — Align calendars (common trading days)
# ----------------------------------------
# Why:
# - BTC trades every day (including weekends)
# - NASDAQ/DXY trade mostly weekdays
# - For regression, we want dates where all variables exist
# Inner join = keep only dates where all variables exist.
# - Hence, INNER merges will be used (common dates only)

# Now it will be merged step-by-step using Date as the key


# Step 2.d — Merge BTC and NASDAQ (1:1 validation + merge indicator)
# ----------------------------------------
# validate='1:1' ensures each Date appears at most once in each dataset
# indicator=True creates a _merge column showing how rows matched

df = pd.merge(
    btc, nasdaq,
    on="Date",
    how="inner",
    validate="1:1",
    indicator=True
)

df["_merge"].value_counts(), df.head()


# Step 2.e — Merge DXY into the dataset
# Like we merged BTC and NASDAQ, we merge DXY using an inner join to keep only common dates.

df = pd.merge(
    df.drop(columns=["_merge"]),  # remove old indicator to avoid confusion
    dxy,
    on="Date",
    how="inner",
    validate="1:1",
    indicator=True
)

df["_merge"].value_counts(), df.head()


# Step 2.f — Now Merge Fed Funds (daily resampled) into the dataset

df = pd.merge(
    df.drop(columns=["_merge"]),
    fed_daily,
    on="Date",
    how="inner",
    validate="1:1",
    indicator=True
)

df["_merge"].value_counts(), df.head(), df.tail()


# Step 2.g — Post-merge quality check
# check for missing values and final shape of the dataset

df.isna().sum(), df.shape


# Step 2.h — Export aligned dataset (processed)
# Useful for transparency + teamwork and for future steps (e.g., return calculations, regression)

df = df.drop(columns=["_merge"], errors="ignore")  # remove merge flag before saving and ignore if it doesn't exist
# We drop the _merge column before saving since it's only for debugging/inspection during merging.
# Create directory if it doesn't exist (it avoids errors when saving)
import os

os.makedirs("data/processed", exist_ok=True)

df.to_csv("data/processed/aligned_prices.csv", index=False)
df.to_csv("data/processed/aligned_prices.csv", index=False)

df.head(), df.tail()


# Step 2.I, CLARIFICATION, Actually, previous to the output from the step 2.h, the fed_rate was returning twice the colums--
# --indicating it was merged twice before, so in the following cell, the code--
# df["fed_rate"] = df["fed_rate_x"] was run to check if the different/duplicate columns were identical,-- 
# -- and if they were (which they were), the duplicate column was dropped with 
# df.drop(columns=["fed_rate_x", "fed_rate_y"], inplace=True
# Now this cannot be seen in the code above because it was fixed before the final output,
# but it is worth noting that this issue was encountered and resolved during the data cleaning process.


# STEP 3 — Feature Engineering
# ----------------------------------------
# Step 3.a — Compute daily log returns
# Why:
# - Returns remove trend from price levels
# - Log returns are standard in financial econometrics
# - We use diff(log(price)) ≈ percentage change

import numpy as np

df["btc_ret"] = np.log(df["btc_price"]).diff()
df["nasdaq_ret"] = np.log(df["nasdaq_price"]).diff()
df["dxy_ret"] = np.log(df["dxy_price"]).diff()

df[["Date", "btc_ret", "nasdaq_ret", "dxy_ret"]].head()


# Step 3.b — Compute daily change in Fed Funds rate
# Why:
# - Markets react to rate changes, not static levels 
# - First difference makes the series dynamic

df["fed_change"] = df["fed_rate"].diff()
(
    df[["Date", "fed_rate", "fed_change"]].head(10),
    df[["Date", "fed_rate", "fed_change"]].tail(10)
)


# Step 3.c — Remove NA values from differencing.
# In previous outputs (3.a and 3.b) it can be seen that returns + fed_change introduced NA in first row,
# so we drop NA values to have a clean dataset for regression and analysis.

df = df.dropna().reset_index(drop=True)

df.shape


# Step 3.d — 30-day rolling correlation (BTC vs NASDAQ)
# # Measures time-varying relationship between Bitcoin and equity market (NASDAQ)
# Shows how relationship evolves over time

df["rolling_corr_btc_nasdaq"] = (
    df["btc_ret"]
      .rolling(window=30)
      .corr(df["nasdaq_ret"])
)

df[["Date", "rolling_corr_btc_nasdaq"]].tail()


# Step 3.E – Rolling 30-day correlation (BTC vs DXY)
# Tests whether Bitcoin behaves inversely to dollar strength

df["corr_btc_dxy"] = (
    df["btc_ret"]
    .rolling(window=30)
    .corr(df["dxy_ret"])
)

df[["Date", "corr_btc_dxy"]].tail()


# Step 3.f — Summary statistics of engineered features
df[["btc_ret","nasdaq_ret","dxy_ret","fed_change"]].describe()


# Step 4 - Statistical Analysis & Visualization

# Step 4.a – Correlation Matrix (Preliminary Relationship Assessment)

# This step evaluates the linear association between Bitcoin returns
# and the selected macro-financial variables.
# It provides initial descriptive evidence before formal regression.
# Note: Correlation does NOT imply causation.

corr_matrix = df[["btc_ret", "nasdaq_ret", "dxy_ret", "fed_change"]].corr()

corr_matrix


# Step 4.b – OLS Regression Model

# Objective:
# Estimate the sensitivity (beta coefficients) of Bitcoin returns
# to macro-financial factors:
#   - NASDAQ returns (risk sentiment proxy)
#   - DXY returns (US dollar strength proxy)
#   - Fed Funds changes (monetary policy shock proxy)
#
# Model specification:
#   BTC_t = α + β1*NASDAQ_t + β2*DXY_t + β3*FedChange_t + ε_t
#
# OLS estimates the average marginal effect of each variable
# while holding the others constant.

import statsmodels.api as sm

# Define independent variables (macro factors)
X = df[["nasdaq_ret", "dxy_ret", "fed_change"]]

# Add constant term (intercept α)
X = sm.add_constant(X)

# Define dependent variable (Bitcoin returns)
y = df["btc_ret"]

# Fit Ordinary Least Squares model
model = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()

# Display regression summary
model.summary()


# Step 4.c.1 – 30-Day Rolling Correlation (BTC vs NASDAQ) - Taken from step 3.d but now plotted for visualization.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# This measures the time-varying relationship between Bitcoin
# and equity market risk sentiment.
# A rolling window allows us to observe whether correlation
# strengthens during crises or weakens during decoupling periods.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.figure()
plt.plot(df["Date"], df["rolling_corr_btc_nasdaq"])
plt.axhline(0)
plt.title("30-Day Rolling Correlation: BTC vs NASDAQ")
plt.xlabel("Date")
plt.ylabel("Correlation")
plt.show()


# Step 4.c.2 – 30-Day Rolling Correlation (BTC vs DXY) - Taken from step 3.e but now plotted for visualization.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# This examines whether Bitcoin behaves inversely to the US dollar.
# Negative correlation suggests Bitcoin may act as a dollar hedge,
# while positive correlation suggests risk-on co-movement.

plt.figure()
plt.plot(df["Date"], df["corr_btc_dxy"])
plt.axhline(0)
plt.title("30-Day Rolling Correlation: BTC vs DXY")
plt.xlabel("Date")
plt.ylabel("Correlation")
plt.show()

text:
Types of Merges
Four main types of merges (similar to SQL joins):

Inner join: Only matching rows from both DataFrames
Left join: All rows from left DataFrame, matching from right
Right join: All rows from right DataFrame, matching from left
Outer join: All rows from both DataFrames

Understanding these is crucial for combining datasets correctly!

title: Python for Data Management
text:
Merge Validation Options
The validate parameter helps catch data quality issues:

'1:1': One-to-one (each key appears once in each DataFrame)
'1:m': One-to-many (left keys unique, right keys can repeat)
'm:1': Many-to-one (left keys can repeat, right keys unique)
'm:m': Many-to-many (keys can repeat in both)

Best practice: Always use validate when you know the expected relationship!

# Use validate parameter
pd.merge(df1, df2, on='id', validate='1:1')  # Will issue error if duplicates

# Standardize before merging

Problem 3: Different data types
# Convert to same type
df1['year'] = df1['year'].astype(int)
df2['year'] = df2['year'].astype(int)
Always know what your data should look like in theory…

name: Deploy to GitHub Pages

on:

jobs:
  deploy:

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v2
      
      - name: Build site
        run: |
          # Your build commands here
          npm install
